office.title: Indiana County Sheriff
office.summary: The sheriff is an elected county officer created by the Indiana Constitution who arrests offenders, keeps the peace, serves court papers, keeps order in county courts and runs the county jail [1, 2]. The Indiana Sheriffs' Association describes sheriffs as constitutional officers elected by the people, whose work includes operating jails, serving civil process, providing court security and coordinating emergency response [3]. Every county elects its sheriff in 2026 for a four-year term, and no one may serve as sheriff more than eight years in any twelve-year period [1].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years; the sheriff serves until a successor is elected and qualified [4, 1]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: Countywide by the county's voters on the partisan general election ballot; all county sheriffs are elected in 2026 [1]

facts.label: Term limit
facts.value: No more than eight years in any period of twelve years (Indiana Constitution, Article 6, Section 2) [1]

facts.label: Qualifications
facts.value: Must have lived in the county for at least one year before the election, be registered to vote in the county by the filing deadline, and file a statement of economic interests; a sheriff who moves out of the county forfeits the office [1, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: A county may pay the sheriff a salary from the county general fund of at least 50% to 100% of the state minimum salary of a full-time prosecuting attorney, depending on county population [5]

duties: Arrests without a warrant people who commit an offense in the sheriff's view, brings them before a county court, and holds them while the arrest is investigated [2].
Suppresses breaches of the peace and pursues and jails felons [2].
Takes care of the county jail and the prisoners held there [2, 3].
Serves and carries out legal papers (process) directed to the sheriff by courts and the county commissioners [2].
Attends and keeps order in all courts of the county, which the Sheriffs' Association describes as providing court security [2, 3].
Takes photographs, fingerprints and other identification data from people held for crimes, and DNA samples for felonies [2].
Reports twice a year to the Indiana Department of Correction the average daily cost of holding a jail prisoner [2].
Holds state prisoners, including people convicted of Level 6 felonies, in the county jail, for which the state reimburses counties at a daily rate set in the state budget [7].
Coordinates emergency response and works with local police, prosecutors and community partners [3].

In a county whose council creates a sheriff's merit board by ordinance, appoints three of its five members, while the county police officers elect the other two; no more than two sheriff appointees and one elected member may belong to the same party [8].

Must report information to federal authorities when a person arrested for a felony or misdemeanor is believed to lack legal immigration status, and, since July 2026, notify the judge setting bail when holding a person subject to an immigration detainer [9, 10].
May supervise and inspect businesses such as pawnbrokers and secondhand dealers [2].

What the sheriff does not control: the county commissioners must establish and maintain the county jail building [11]; the county makes the appropriation for feeding prisoners and sets the sheriff's salary [5]; the prosecuting attorney decides which crimes to prosecute [12]; and judges decide bail [13].
recent_changes: February 2025: The Indiana Department of Correction said funding to reimburse county jails for holding Level 6 felons and state prisoners, then $40 per day, was exhausted for state fiscal year 2025; Tippecanoe County Sheriff Robert Goldsmith, then president of the Indiana Sheriffs' Association, called it very disappointing, and Rep. Greg Steuerwald (R-Avon) said everything owed would be paid [14].

2025: The new state budget raised the daily rate for Level 6 offenders to $42, raised the jail reimbursement line to $45 million and then $41 million a year, and moved to direct reimbursement with costs submitted within 60 days; Sheriffs' Association executive director Stephen Luce called the rate better than nothing, citing an association study that put the average cost at about $74 per inmate per day [7].
July 2025: The Department of Correction planned to begin paying about $12.7 million owed to county jails for housing state offenders [7].

July 2025: House Enrolled Act 1393 took effect, requiring jails to alert federal immigration authorities, with the county sheriff passing the information to federal officials, after felony or misdemeanor arrests when there is probable cause the person lacks legal status [9].

July 2026: Senate Bill 76 took effect, requiring sheriff's offices and police departments to notify the bail judge when they hold a person subject to an immigration detainer and barring local policies that restrict cooperation with federal officials; St. Joseph County Sheriff Bill Redman said his county already cooperates with ICE, while South Bend Mayor James Mueller said the city will protect the constitutional rights of everyone living there [10].

January 2026: The Sheriffs' Association's 2026 president, Porter County Sheriff Jeffrey Balon, listed jail overcrowding, staffing shortages, the drug epidemic and mental illness among the issues sheriffs raise with legislators [3].

November 2026: Public Question 1 asks voters whether courts may deny bail, for offenses other than murder or treason, when the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect others or the community [15]; Sen. Eric Koch (R-Bedford) said releasing some defendants before trial is too dangerous, while Zach Stock of the Indiana Public Defender Council raised concerns about jail overcrowding [13].

incumbent.name: John L. Beeman
incumbent.summary: John Beeman, a Republican, has been Madison County sheriff since the end of December 2022 and is seeking a second consecutive term; he won the Republican nomination in the May 5, 2026 primary over three challengers [16, 17, 18].
record: December 31, 2022: Beeman took office as sheriff after a 30-year career with the U.S. Marshals Service, according to his campaign [16].

Office profile: the sheriff's department lists a jail built in 1984 with a capacity of 207 offenders and 45 jail officers, seven criminal investigators plus two Madison County Drug Task Force detectives, three full-time victim advocates, and a 450-square-mile patrol area [19].

September 2025: Asked about holding people for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Beeman told Woof Boom News that people are 'not held here solely for immigration'; he said they are typically arrested on local charges, and ICE is contacted before release only if the person shows up in the system as wanted for immigration violations [20].

March 2026: Beeman's campaign described a new $110.5 million jail and the repurposing of the Madison County Community Corrections work-release center, and said he wants to 'consolidate and streamline jail operations for the 2030s and beyond' [21].

First term, per his campaign: it lists completing 'Phase 2' of the new jail, jail mental-health and addiction treatment paid for with opioid settlement funds, 24-hour jail medical coverage, 12-hour jail shifts to reduce overtime, support for a 21% raise for merit deputies and a 22% raise for jail staff, full authorized staffing, a school resource officer for East Elementary School, five vehicles bought with non-taxpayer funds, and bullet-resistant windshields for patrol cars. These are the campaign's own claims [22].

April 2026: Beeman's campaign said arrests for violent and property crimes 'have fallen to levels not seen in many years' and that the department 'already operates on the leanest possible budget'; the post cites no figures or data source [23].

race_context: Madison County (Anderson) elects its sheriff to four-year terms; Sheriff John Beeman, first elected in 2022, is running for a second consecutive term, so this is not an open seat [16, 18].
In the May 5, 2026 Republican primary, official county results show Beeman with 3,991 votes (about 43%), Brian K. Bell 2,298, Kimberly Stigall 1,504 and Jonathan Culp 1,384 [17].
In the Democratic primary, Anderson Police Assistant Chief Norman Rayford Jr. received 3,701 votes (about 54%) to Dennis Watson's 3,171 [17].
WLBC reported that a Beeman win would make him the first Republican to win two consecutive terms as Madison County sheriff since John Gunter, elected in 1970 and 1974 [18].

Issues for the office include the move from the 1984 jail (rated for 207) to a new jail, jail staffing and pay, and the county budget; Beeman's campaign says it expects falling county tax revenue in 2027 [19, 21, 24].
Both nominees are career law-enforcement officers: Beeman in federal service before becoming sheriff, Rayford with the Anderson Police Department since the late 1990s [16, 25].
No general-election candidate forum or debate for this race was found in the sources reviewed.

candidates.summary: John Beeman is the Republican incumbent sheriff, in office since December 2022, after a 30-year career with the U.S. Marshals Service; he won a four-way Republican primary in May 2026 [16, 17].
background: His campaign says he served in the U.S. Army from 1984 to 1988, graduated from Ball State University, and spent 30 years with the U.S. Marshals Service, including as supervisory inspector over the Great Lakes Regional Fugitive Task Force in Indianapolis from 2007 [16].
Co-owner of Gunslingers, a gun shop in Anderson [26].
path_to_ballot: Won the Republican nomination in the May 5, 2026 primary with 3,991 votes, ahead of Brian K. Bell (2,298), Kimberly Stigall (1,504) and Jonathan Culp (1,384) [17].

items: Says his federal experience in jail operations, judicial security and prisoner operations will help ensure a safe transition to the new jail; plans to consolidate and streamline jail operations and repurpose the community corrections work-release center [21].
Lists opioid-settlement-funded mental-health and addiction treatment in the jail and 24-hour jail medical coverage among his first-term steps [22].
Says he will keep pressing to make pay competitive so trained jail staff and experienced merit deputies are not lost to nearby cities and counties that pay more [24].
Cites support for raises of 21% (merit deputies) and 22% (jail staff) and moving jail staff to 12-hour shifts to reduce overtime [22].
Says he will prepare for expected falling county tax revenue in 2027 and keep urging the county council to prioritize public-safety funding [24].
Says 'every dollar of the Sheriff's budget is voted on and approved by the County Council' [23].
Said people are not held in the county jail solely for immigration status; ICE is contacted before release only when someone is listed as wanted for immigration violations [20].
Lists adding a school resource officer for East Elementary School [22].

on_incumbent: His campaign refers to 'a two-year crime surge from 2018 to 2022 during the previous Sheriff's administration'; it does not cite figures [23].
No statements by Beeman about his general-election opponent were found.
plans: Finish modernizing the department, carry out the plan for the new jail once completed, and continue consolidating jail staff [24, 21].
endorsements_finance: His campaign says his endorsements 'come from all walks of life' but does not name endorsers [27].
gaps: No campaign finance totals were found; Madison County's website does not post candidate finance reports.

Beeman's campaign site describes him in different places as the first Republican sheriff since 1978 (search snippet only) and since 1982 (About page); WLBC frames it as the first Republican to win consecutive terms since 1970/1974. Not reconciled.

Current status of the new jail (opening date, final bed count) was not confirmed from a free source; search snippets from syndicated articles mention a 525-bed facility and a September 2026 completion target, unverified.

Search snippets (unverified) said Beeman requested funding for six correctional officers in 2024 and six in 2025 and that both requests were cut by the county council, and that the jail held six ICE detainees in 2025; the underlying articles are Herald Bulletin content and were not used.
No 287(g) agreement was found in the sources reviewed.
His 2022 general-election vote totals were not retrieved.
Herald Bulletin coverage of the race is paywalled and was not used.

candidates.summary: Norman Rayford Jr. is assistant chief of the Anderson Police Department, where he has served for more than two decades; he won the Democratic nomination in May 2026 over Dennis Watson [25, 17].
background: Assistant chief (Uniform Division) of the Anderson Police Department since April 4, 2022, overseeing patrol personnel, the crash team, K9 units and SWAT [25].

Has served with the Anderson Police Department for more than 23 years, with assignments in community policing, the traffic division, the criminal investigation division and as a shift sergeant; named Law Enforcement Officer of the Year in 2017 [25].
path_to_ballot: Won the Democratic nomination in the May 5, 2026 primary with 3,701 votes to Dennis Watson's 3,171 [17].
Told the Oldies 101 program 'Anderson Talks' that he had bipartisan encouragement to enter the primary [28].
on_incumbent: No statements by Rayford about Sheriff Beeman's record were found in the free sources reviewed.
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found.
gaps: Coverage of Rayford's platform is thin in free sources; no campaign website was found, and the Civoren profile lists no positions.

Search snippets of a syndicated Herald Bulletin article (not used) said Rayford wants the department to be more open with the public, said some past cases 'were not handled appropriately,' and wants to upgrade vehicles and address budget issues tied to the new jail; unverified.

Search snippets (unverified) said he has been with the Anderson Police Department since 1999 and served as president of Fraternal Order of Police Local 48; the department page reviewed did not mention the FOP role.
The 'Anderson Talks' interview audio (about March 30, 2026) was not reviewed.
No campaign finance totals were found; Madison County's website does not post candidate finance reports.
